profile.address: 215 East Indian School Road, Phoenix, AZ 85012
profile.reading:
This is a small, old, urban telephone building that now sells colocation, and the county record makes that plain. Maricopa County assessor parcel 118-25-125 contains this record's coordinates and carries the situs address 215 East Indian School Road, Phoenix, Arizona 85012. The county places it in legal class 1.11, telecommunications, under property use code 5600, telecommunications property. The lot is 54,530 square feet, about 1.25 acres. That is a central office footprint on a central Phoenix corner, not a wholesale campus on the edge of the valley. The registered owner is recorded as Qwest, with a mailing address at 6300 South Syracuse Way, Englewood, Colorado, the tax office that has followed the old US West and Qwest local exchange estate through every corporate name since. The deed on file was recorded in 2001. The county's ZIP for the parcel is 85012, not the 85013 this registry previously carried.

Lumen Technologies is what that estate is called now. CenturyLink acquired Qwest in 2011, acquired Level 3 Communications on 1 November 2017, renamed itself Lumen on 14 September 2020 and changed its ticker from CTL to LUMN four days later. Lumen sells this kind of building as network colocation rather than as wholesale data centre space. Its own colocation data sheet claims more than 175 carrier neutral data centres across more than 60 North American markets and quotes cabinet power in a 3 to 15 kilowatt range that it says varies by site. Lumen publishes no square footage, no megawatt figure and no address for any individual site, and this one is no exception.

The county roll shows something worth pointing at. The parcel carries a land full cash value of $3,271,800 and no improvement value at all. The building is standing and in service, but its value is not on the local roll, which is consistent with Arizona treating telecommunications company property separately from ordinary locally assessed commercial property. The Arizona Department of Revenue publishes a dedicated telecommunications company property tax form, Form 82056, filed under A.R.S. sections 42-14001 to 42-14005 and 42-14401 to 42-14404. The practical consequence for this registry is that the county cannot supply the building square footage or improvement value it supplies for a conventional data centre parcel.

Phoenix adopted its first zoning definition of a data centre only on 2 July 2025, decades after this exchange was placed in service, and the debate that produced it is not about buildings like this one. Arizona Public Service reports an uncommitted queue of 19.0 gigawatts of large load requests against data centres making up about 5 percent of its 2025 peak. At the Arizona Corporation Commission's large load workshop on 16 April 2026, staff counted about two dozen operating data centres in Arizona with more than 2,000 MW of operating capacity and more than 10,600 MW planned. A 1.25 acre telephone building with a few hundred cabinets sits at the opposite end of that distribution and is easy to mistake for the thing being argued about.

What is not known: no IT load, utility service capacity or standby generation figure is published for this site, the electric utility serving the parcel was not confirmed from a primary source, and the building's floor area does not appear in the county record.

Lumen Albany 4 is a network colocation site at 10 Airline Drive in the Town of Colonie, in the Albany metropolitan area of New York, mapped here as a point rather than a building outline. It is not a hyperscale campus and should not be read as one. Lumen Technologies, formerly CenturyLink, which took the Lumen name on September 14, 2020 and the LUMN ticker four days later, and which absorbed Level 3 Communications in a deal that closed November 1, 2017, sells this class of site as carrier neutral edge colocation attached to its own long haul network. Lumen's published colocation material describes more than 175 such facilities across more than 60 North American markets and quotes cabinet power in a 3 to 15 kilowatt band that varies by site. It publishes no square footage, no total megawatt figure and no individual street address for any of them, which is why the facility code Albany 4 is the most specific identifier available.

The local property record is worth reporting because of what it does not contain. The Town of Colonie assessment roll lists parcels at 4, 6, 8, 10A, 10B, 10C, 11, 12, 12A and 13 Airline Drive, under owners including a private realty group, an office trust and a school district body, but no parcel numbered simply 10, and no parcel on that street owned by Lumen, CenturyLink or Level 3. The Lumen group appears in the roll only in the sections for network property, as special franchise parcel 99.55-6-11 in property class 866 for telephone, assessed at 575,338 dollars under the name Level 3 Telecom NY care of the CenturyLink property tax department in Broomfield, Colorado, and in the utility and railroad section as class 836 telecommunications equipment described as outside plant and fiber optic cable spread across the South Colonie, North Colonie, Niskayuna and Mohonasen school districts. The straightforward reading is that Lumen occupies leased space in a building it does not own and pays tax on its network plant rather than on real property here. Which of the Airline Drive parcels holds the suite is not established, so no owner, improvement square footage or year built is recorded on this page.

New York's regulatory posture toward data centers changed sharply in 2026, and the interesting question for a site like this one is whether any of it reaches it. Executive Order 62, signed July 14, 2026, defines a data center as a facility that consumes or can consume 50 megawatts or more, directs the Department of Environmental Conservation to hold incomplete permit applications for such facilities in abeyance, and runs until the Department of Public Service delivers a final generic environmental impact statement, with carve outs for manufacturing, research, education, medical uses and the Empire AI consortium. A colocation site quoting cabinet power in kilowatts is almost certainly far below that line. This Lumen colocation facility is located at 1757 Old Meadow Road, McLean, VA 22102, one of two adjacent Lumen buildings on Old Meadow Road (the other at 1755, also tracked in this registry), part of the broader Tysons/McLean data center and telecommunications corridor near Washington, DC; Lumen does not publish individual building addresses or specs on its own site for any of its 175-plus North American colocation sites. Lumen Technologies, formerly CenturyLink (renamed Lumen on September 14, 2020, with its stock ticker changing from CTL to LUMN on September 18, 2020) and built in part on CenturyLink's November 1, 2017 acquisition of Level 3 Communications, operates this facility as part of a network-centric edge colocation product rather than a wholesale hyperscale campus. Lumen's own colocation data sheet states more than 175 carrier-neutral data centers across more than 60 North American markets, offering cabinet power in the 3 to 15 kilowatt range described as varying by site; unlike the wholesale operators tracked elsewhere in this registry, Lumen does not disclose per-building square footage or total MW capacity for any of its sites.

Virginia's data center boom is reshaping statewide electricity rates directly relevant to every Northern Virginia facility. In November 2026, the Virginia State Corporation Commission approved new Dominion Energy rates that will raise a typical residential bill by about $16 a month to roughly $165, while creating a new GS-5 rate class specifically for data centers effective January 1, 2027; regulators approved $775.6 million of the roughly $1.2 billion Dominion sought, cutting about $350 million tied to speculative data center projects, according to Inside Climate News.

The Tysons/McLean corridor has long served as a network interconnection hub for the Washington, DC metro, predating much of the newer hyperscale build-out further west in Loudoun County; Lumen's two adjacent Old Meadow Road buildings reflect that older, carrier-hotel-style pattern of data center development.

Lumen Technologies is a public company trading as LUMN, SEC filer CIK 0000018926, headquartered in Denver, Colorado. The company was previously known as CenturyLink and absorbed Level 3 Communications after CenturyLink acquired it in 2017, before adopting the Lumen name.

Lumen's own about page describes the company as a global communications services provider built around a global fiber network, citing service-level figures such as wavelengths up to 400 gigabits per second and dedicated internet access up to 100 gigabits per second, but the fetched page did not state a company-wide data center count or capacity total. Recent 2026 trade press reports Lumen selling its Broomfield, Colorado office campus for $15 million, a former secondary office location rather than its current Denver headquarters.

The registry here tracks 19 Lumen facilities across twelve states, Arizona, California, Maryland, Minnesota, Nevada, New York, Pennsylvania, Texas, Utah, Virginia, Washington, and Wisconsin. Unlike the colocation REITs and hyperscalers elsewhere in this registry, Lumen's data centers function primarily as network edge and interconnection points supporting its fiber and telecommunications business, rather than as the company's core commercial product, so its facility footprint should be read as a distributed network-edge presence rather than a wholesale colocation portfolio comparable to Digital Realty's or Equinix's.
